hallgrimsson-israel-intimidate-ireland.headline: Hallgrímsson says Israel 'tried to intimidate' Ireland amid spitting row
hallgrimsson-israel-intimidate-ireland.body_md:
Ireland manager Heimir Hallgrímsson said Israel tried to intimidate his side from the first whistle in a bad-tempered Nations League draw on Sunday. The match was overshadowed by an allegation that a member of Ireland's staff was spat at during the interval.

The game finished 1-1 at the TSC Arena in Bačka Topola, Serbia, a neutral venue where it was played behind closed doors. Troy Parrott put Ireland ahead with a first-half penalty. Dor Peretz equalised for Israel.

## The row at half-time

The flashpoint came as the teams left the pitch at the break. The Irish Times reported that Damien Doyle, Ireland's head of athletic performance, alleged an Israel player had spat on him. On television pictures, a voice can be heard saying "he spat on me" as the players headed down the tunnel.

Hallgrímsson did not dwell on the incident itself, but he was blunt about the wider pattern of the match.

> "I felt like they were trying to intimidate us from kick-off but I give a lot of credit to the players to stay calm."

His praise for his players' composure is the notable part. A game with this much friction can easily produce cards, and Ireland avoided the kind of reaction that would have changed the result.

## Israel's response

Israel's head coach, Ran Ben-Shimon, said he "didn't see anything". He explained he was in the dressing room with his staff when the incident was alleged to have happened. Asked about the physical treatment of Ireland midfielder Jason Molumby, he said it was "nothing personal" and that his team does not instruct players to injure opponents.

The accounts do not conflict as directly as the headlines suggest. Ben-Shimon is not disputing that the tunnel exchange took place. He is saying he was not there to see it. The allegation rests on Doyle's account and on the audio picked up by the broadcast. No finding has been published, and Israel has not been reported to have responded to the specific claim beyond the manager's comments.

## Why the tension

These are the second meeting between the sides in a matter of weeks. Ireland won the first, 3-0 in Hungary last month. Both fixtures have been staged away from Israel and carry the weight of the wider political climate around the Gaza conflict. The Football Association of Ireland is also reported to be looking into alleged racial abuse of Adam Idah by Israel supporters at the first game.

Whether UEFA opens disciplinary proceedings over the half-time allegation is the next thing to watch. The governing body typically asks for match-delegate and referee reports before deciding whether to charge anyone. Any evidence from the tunnel footage would be central to that.

f1-timing-glitch-lego-race.headline: Hamilton bemused as F1 timing glitch turns race into a 'Lego race'
f1-timing-glitch-lego-race.body_md:
The race was supposed to be the story. Instead, a software fault that left cars crawling and stalling in the wet at Sepang took over, and Lewis Hamilton, who finished third, was left describing the afternoon as 'like the Lego race'.

The glitch was in the cars, not the television broadcast. The fault hit the power-unit software and affected several drivers during the formation laps behind the safety car. Cars that should have been rolling at a steady pace instead lost power or struggled to move at normal speed.

## What happened

Hamilton said he had to stop on the track, switch off the car and the engine, and restart it. 'I've never done that before,' he said. At one point five cars were reported side by side on the straight, with drivers unable to work out what was happening ahead of them.

The 'Lego race' line is a reference to the battery-powered Lego F1 cars that took part in a promotional show before the British Grand Prix in July. Max Verstappen, who is reported to have won the race, used the same comparison and put the cause down to complexity. 'These engines are so complicated and a lot of software is implemented,' he said.

## The cause

According to the reports, the FIA traced the fault to an unusual combination of conditions: low engine speeds, low grip, the energy-management settings used in the wet, and the layout of one part of the Sepang circuit. Together these triggered an unintended loss of power in several cars.

The governing body issued updated software during the rain delay. It removed the energy limit in the affected sectors before the race resumed. Reports say the FIA, teams and power-unit manufacturers will now review why the problem was not caught earlier. Rain-affected running has been scarce this season, which would explain how a wet-weather combination went untested.

## Why it matters, and why not very much

The fault was fixed within the same event, and nothing in the accounts suggests the result was distorted. A wet race restarted after a delay with corrected software is an ordinary, if embarrassing, outcome.

The more lasting point is about the 2026 rules. The current engines lean heavily on software to manage electrical energy deployment. That makes them more exposed to rare combinations of conditions like these than the old hardware-dominated units were. One bug on a wet afternoon does not show a systemic flaw. It does show that the software now needs wet-weather testing as seriously as the engines themselves.

The review is the next thing to watch. If it concludes the fault was a one-off gap in wet-weather testing, the story ends here. If it finds other untested conditions, the teams will want answers before the next rainy race weekend.

missing-plane-us-coast-presumed-dead.headline: Missing plane off US coast: all six aboard presumed dead
missing-plane-us-coast-presumed-dead.body_md:
A Canadian air ambulance that vanished on its way from Bermuda to Boston has been given up for lost. The US Coast Guard suspended its search at sunset on Sunday, 66 hours after the Gulfstream G100 dropped off radar. All six people aboard are presumed dead.

The flight, callsign Heartbeat 104, was a medical transfer. According to NBC News, it was operated by Canada-based Latitude Air Ambulance. Four Canadian crew members were aboard, along with two Bermudians: a patient and the patient's son, who was travelling as a family escort. The jet left L.F. Wade International Airport in Bermuda in the small hours of Saturday and was due at Boston Logan before 1:30 a.m.

It never arrived.

## The last minutes

The Federal Aviation Administration lost contact with the aircraft as it descended over the Atlantic, south of Nantucket. NBC reports the jet dropped from 24,000 feet to about 11,000 feet before contact was lost. ABC News, citing air traffic audio, reports the pilot had described electrical problems and declared an emergency. Aviation analyst Mary Schiavo told ABC the recordings suggest the aircraft was "coming in blind" as a storm moved across its path. That is informed speculation rather than a finding. Investigators have not said what went wrong.

Searchers later found a debris field roughly 20 miles off Nantucket. Coast Guard fixed-wing aircraft, helicopters, boats and cutters combed the water, supported by Massachusetts authorities and the New York National Guard. Reports differ on how large the search area was, and on exactly when contact was lost, so those figures are best treated as approximate.

## Why the search stopped

Rear Adm. Matthew Lake, whose district ran the operation, said ending a search was never a simple call.

> "Suspending a search is not an easy decision. We express our deepest condolences to the families."

The debris sits in comparatively shallow water, ABC reports 80 to 90 feet. That makes recovery of the wreckage, and of the flight recorders, plausible. The Coast Guard had said it planned to use sonar to scan the seabed. NBC says no black box has yet been located.

## What comes next

The US National Transportation Safety Board is expected to lead the inquiry, with Canada's Transportation Safety Board taking part, since the aircraft was Canadian-registered and the crew Canadian. The first thing to watch is whether the wreck and its recorders are found. They would show whether an electrical failure, the weather, or both brought the jet down. An NTSB preliminary report would normally follow within a few weeks.

Air ambulance flights carry people already in fragile health, over open water, often at night. When one is lost, it is a loss for the families and for the medical-transport crews who fly the same routes.

trump-super-intelligence-force.headline: Trump unveils 'Super Intelligence Force' to oversee AI policy
trump-super-intelligence-force.body_md:
The White House has created a new body to coordinate federal AI policy and given it a name borrowed from science fiction: the "Super Intelligence Force". Announced on 4 October, it has a named leader, a short list of cabinet-level members and a 120-day reporting deadline. Nothing in the published accounts gives it a budget line, regulatory authority or any way to compel a company or agency to do anything.

## What was announced

Donald Trump said Jay Clayton, the Director of National Intelligence, will lead the force. According to a summary of the announcement by Straight Arrow News, its members include Vice President JD Vance, Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth, Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent and chief of staff Susie Wiles. Its stated job is to coordinate government engagement with AI developers, consumers, religious organisations and infrastructure providers.

It has to report within 120 days on AI risks, opportunities, security vulnerabilities and how breaches should be reported. That is a deliverable, not a power. A report due in early February can recommend rules, but it cannot make them.

Trump also signed an executive order directing federal agencies to say "super intelligence" instead of "artificial intelligence". His reasoning, as reported, was that "artificial" makes the technology sound "fake, and it is not fake, it's actually amazing." Clayton's own line was more conventional: "The risk of not being first is high."

The Washington Post framed the launch as coming after calls for an AI slowdown. That suggests the body is as much a political answer to safety critics as a regulatory step. The claim rests on that framing and on the thin remit, not on any stated administration motive.

## Why the market impact looks limited

Coordinating bodies of this kind have a mixed record. They tend to hold meetings, commission reports and rely on the agencies that already have the legal authority. Without money or enforcement tools, they lose influence once the political attention moves elsewhere or budgets tighten.

What would change the picture:

- **Budget authority.** A funding line, or a say over federal AI procurement, would give the body leverage over suppliers.
- **Binding rules.** Reporting requirements for security breaches, for example, would turn the 120-day review into obligations for companies.
- **Chip and export policy.** The members include the Treasury and Defense secretaries. If the force starts shaping those decisions, that would matter more to valuations than the name does.

None of these is in the announcement. Clayton's background is in securities law and intelligence, not the technology industry, which critics have noted. That may suit a security-focused review, but it says little about how much the body will shape policy.

The backdrop is nervous. Bank of England governor Andrew Bailey said this week that "everybody is currently priced to be a winner" as AI-linked debt nears $450bn. A Washington body with no powers is unlikely to move prices on its own. A later move that gives it some could.

## The rebrand has a side effect

The rename has already had a small commercial effect. BBC Technology reported a spike in demand for Slovenian domain names. The country's ".si" suffix looks like the start of "super intelligence", which has sent buyers looking for addresses. We could not independently confirm the scale of that demand.

## What to watch

The first marker is the 120-day report, due around early February. The more important test comes sooner: whether the White House attaches funding, staff or a legal mandate to the force, or whether the order stays a renaming exercise.
